Édouard Philippe: Prime Minister of France from 2017 to 2020. A lawyer by occupation, Philippe is a former member of the Union for a Popular Movement (UMP), which later became The Republicans (LR).

Joseph Schumpeter (born 1883) is the earliest of the four. Joseph Alois Schumpeter (German: [ˈʃʊmpeːtɐ]; February 8, 1883 – January 8, 1950) was an Austrian political economist.
Who among these four was born earliest?
Jabir ibn Hayyan (born 721) is the earliest of the four. The c. 215 treatises that survive today mainly deal with alchemy and chemistry, magic, and Shi'ite religious philosophy.
Which of these four dates back furthest?
Fortran (founded 1957) is the earliest of the four.
Which of these four began earliest?
Pascal (programming language) (founded 1970) is the earliest of the four. It is named after French mathematician, philosopher and physicist Blaise Pascal.
Which one below is best known as a physicist?
John Archibald Wheeler is a physicist. John Archibald Wheeler (July 9, 1911 – April 13, 2008) was an American theoretical physicist.
Pick the mathematician from these four.
Émilie du Châtelet is a mathematician. It circulated widely, generated heated debates, and was translated into German and Italian in 1743.
What is the atomic number of Darmstadtium?
Darmstadtium is a synthetic chemical element; it has symbol Ds and atomic number 110.
What is the atomic number of Gold?
Gold is a chemical element; its chemical symbol is Au (from Latin aurum) and atomic number 79.
In what year did Kitty Oppenheimer die?
Kitty Oppenheimer: Robert Oppenheimer, the director of the Manhattan Project's Los Alamos Laboratory during World War II.
In what year was Boron discovered?
Boron is a chemical element; it has symbol B and atomic number 5.
Dopamine: Pfizer. Dopamine (DA, a contraction of 3,4-dihydroxyphenethylamine) is a neuromodulatory molecule that plays several important roles in cells.
In which country is TAI TF Kaan?
TAI TF Kaan: Turkey. Designed to replace the Turkish Air Force’s fleet of F-16 Fighting Falcons, the Kaan is also intended for export to international markets.
Who is credited with discovering Leo Minor?
Leo Minor: Johannes Hevelius. Leo Minor is a small and faint constellation in the northern celestial hemisphere.
Who is credited with discovering Graph theory?
Graph theory: Leonhard Euler. In mathematics and computer science, graph theory is the study of graphs, which are mathematical structures used to model pairwise relations between objects.
Who is credited with discovering Budesonide?
Budesonide: Ralph Brattsand. Budesonide, sold under the brand name Pulmicort, among others, is a steroid medication.
Who is credited with discovering Platinum?
Platinum: Julius Caesar Scaliger. Platinum is a chemical element; it has symbol Pt and atomic number 78.
A broad-spectrum benzimidazole drug, this medicine clears intestinal parasites from pinworm to hookworm to tapeworm — which agent is it?
Albendazole is a broad-spectrum antihelmintic and antiprotozoal agent of the benzimidazole type.
Famed for foundational work in number theory and algebraic geometry, this French mathematician was also a principal founder of the secretive Bourbaki group — who was he?
André Weil (6 May 1906 - 6 August 1998) was a French mathematician, known for his foundational work in number theory and algebraic geometry.

In 2003, this American mountaineer amputated his own trapped forearm with a dull pocket knife after five days pinned by a boulder in a Utah canyon, then rappelled and hiked miles to safety — who is he?

Aron Ralston (born October 27, 1975) is an American mountaineer, mechanical engineer, and motivational speaker, known for surviving a canyoneering accident in 2003 by cutting off part of his own right arm.
The second-largest living rodents after capybaras, these large semiaquatic mammals of the Northern Hemisphere have webbed back feet, hand-like front paws, and flat, scaly tails — name the animal?
Beaver (genus Castor) are large semiaquatic rodents of the Northern Hemisphere.
Composed mostly of plasma along with red cells, white cells, and platelets, this body fluid ferries oxygen and nutrients to cells while hauling waste away — name the fluid?

Blood is a body fluid in the circulatory system of humans and other vertebrates that delivers necessary substances such as nutrients and oxygen to the cells of the body, and transports metabolic waste products away from those same cells.
The only living group in its tribe, this genus of over 250 fuzzy bees forms small colonies under a single queen — and unlike honeybees, its females can sting again and again — what is it?
Bumblebee (or bumble bee, bumble-bee, or humble-bee) is any of over 250 species in the genus Bombus, part of Apidae, one of the bee families.
Which Mediterranean evergreen tree, grown mainly in Spain, produces edible seed pods often ground into a chocolate substitute, with seeds that yield a gum used as a food thickener?
Carob (Ceratonia siliqua) is a flowering evergreen tree or shrub in the Caesalpinioideae subfamily of the legume family, Fabaceae.
The principal sterol of all animals, it concentrates in the brain and spinal cord and is essential to every cell membrane — yet too much in the blood spells trouble. What is it?
Cholesterol is the principal sterol of all animals, distributed in body tissues, especially the brain and spinal cord, and in animal fats and oils.

The most widely distributed corvid, this large all-black bird is found across the Northern Hemisphere and is the heaviest passerine bird, with 11 accepted subspecies showing little variation in appearance. What bird is this?
Common raven (Corvus corax) is a large all-black passerine bird.
Its name comes from the Greek for "dark blue," and its anion — a carbon triple-bonded to nitrogen — is so toxic that salts like the sodium and potassium forms cause swift poisoning. What is it?
Cyanide (from Greek kyanos 'dark blue') is an inorganic chemical compound that contains a CN functional group.
Known from thousands of fossils pulled from the La Brea Tar Pits, this extinct species of canine roamed the Americas until about 10,000 years ago. Name the species?
Dire wolf (Aenocyon dirus) is an extinct species of canine which was native to the Americas during the Late Pleistocene and Early Holocene epochs (125,000-10,000 years ago).
This mammal family includes living species from two genera as well as extinct giants like the woolly mammoth, and was first scientifically described in 1821 — what family is it?

Elephantidae is a family of large, herbivorous proboscidean mammals which includes the living elephants (belonging to the genera Elephas and Loxodonta), as well as a number of extinct genera like Mammuthus (mammoths) and Palaeoloxodon.

Built by a consortium of Airbus, BAE Systems and Leonardo for four NATO nations, this twin-engine canard delta-wing fighter grew out of the 1983 Future European Fighter Aircraft programme — which jet?
Eurofighter Typhoon is a European multinational twin-engine, supersonic, canard delta wing, multirole fighter.

This genetic neurodevelopmental disorder causes a long, narrow face, large ears, and unusually flexible fingers, with males typically far more affected than females and average IQ under 55 in affected boys — what's the condition?

Fragile X syndrome (FXS) is a genetic neurodevelopmental disorder. The average IQ in males with FXS is under 55, while affected females tend to be in the borderline to normal range, typically around 70–85.
The last living species in an order that first appeared over 290 million years ago, this disease-resistant "living fossil" with fan-shaped leaves is also called the maidenhair tree — which is it?
Ginkgo biloba (-goh), also known as the maidenhair tree, and often misspelled "gingko" (see Etymology below) is a species of gymnosperm tree native to East Asia.
This flatfish's English name blends words for 'holy' and 'flat fish,' a nod to its place on the Catholic holy-day menu. Which bottom-dwelling fish?
Halibut is the common name for three species of flatfish in the family of right-eye flounders.
Nesting monogamously in tree cavities across Africa, Asia, and Melanesia, these birds are unique for having their first two neck vertebrae fused solid — which birds?
Hornbill are birds found in tropical and subtropical Africa, Asia and Melanesia of the family Bucerotidae.

Co-creator of the breakthrough neural network AlexNet and a contributor to landmark AI systems including GPT and AlphaGo, this computer scientist has won a major deep-learning research award three years running — who is he?
Ilya Sutskever (born 1986) is a computer scientist who specializes in machine learning.
This German-American software engineer designed PayPal's real-time anti-fraud system, then co-founded a site whose very first video — "Me at the zoo" — he uploaded himself in April 2005. Who is he?
Jawed Karim (born October 28, 1979) is a German and American software engineer and internet entrepreneur.
This pain-relieving, fever-reducing drug belongs to the propionic acid class of anti-inflammatories and hit the market in 1980, thirteen years after being patented — what is it?
Ketoprofen is one of the propionic acid class of nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAID) with analgesic and antipyretic effects.
This bacterial blood infection, spread between humans, dogs, and rodents, can range from symptomless to a severe form that turns skin and eyes yellow and shuts down the kidneys — what disease is it?
Leptospirosis is a blood infection caused by bacteria of the genus Leptospira that can infect humans, dogs, rodents, and many other wild and domesticated animals.
Born in Vienna into one of Europe's richest families, this philosopher studied under Bertrand Russell at Cambridge and transformed 20th-century philosophy of language and logic — who is he?

Ludwig Wittgenstein ((h)tyne; Austrian; 26 April 1889 - 29 April 1951) was an Austro-British philosopher who worked in logic, philosophy of mathematics, philosophy of mind, and philosophy of language.

In 1835 she and Caroline Herschel became the first female Honorary Members of the Royal Astronomical Society, and decades later this Scottish polymath's name topped John Stuart Mill's women's-suffrage petition. Who is she?
Mary Somerville (ne Fairfax, formerly Greig; 1780-1872) was a Scottish scientist, writer, and polymath.
Built primarily from stainless steel, this Soviet supersonic interceptor could exceed Mach 3.2, but doing so risked wrecking its own engines. What aircraft is it?
Mikoyan-Gurevich MiG-25 (NATO reporting name: Foxbat) is a supersonic interceptor and reconnaissance aircraft that is among the fastest military aircraft to enter service.
This genus of bacteria lacks a cell wall entirely, making it naturally immune to antibiotics like penicillin that target cell-wall synthesis — name this genus?
Mycoplasma is a genus of bacteria that, like the other members of the class Mollicutes, lack a cell wall (peptidoglycan) around their cell membrane.
A child prodigy turned MIT mathematician, this American thinker is considered the originator of cybernetics — the science of communication in living things and machines. Who was he?
Norbert Wiener (November 26, 1894 - March 18, 1964) was an American computer scientist, mathematician, and philosopher.
Often silent at first, this disease arises from an ovary or nearby structures and announces itself only later with bloating, pelvic pain, and abdominal swelling — what is it?
Ovarian cancer is a cancerous tumor of an ovary.
This flowering plant is the sole genus in its own botanical family and ranges from knee-high herbaceous perennials to woody shrubs over ten feet tall — what plant is it?
Peony is any flowering plant in the genus Paeonia, the only genus in the family Paeoniaceae.

This roundworm is one of the most common intestinal parasites in humans, causing a condition sometimes called oxyuriasis after the family it belongs to, and has also been found in bonnet macaques — what's the parasite?
Pinworm (parasite) (species Enterobius vermicularis), also known as threadworm (in the United Kingdom, Australia and New Zealand) or seatworm, is a parasitic worm.
Originating on Gran Canaria and Tenerife, this large Spanish mastiff-type breed was traditionally used to guard property, herd livestock, and, legally until 1936, fight other dogs — what breed is it?
Presa Canario is a Spanish breed of large dog of mastiff or catch dog type.
It can form not just from rain but from mist, spray, or dew, and though we usually see an arc, it can actually be a full circle — what optical phenomenon is it?
Rainbow is an optical phenomenon caused by refraction, internal reflection and dispersion of light in water droplets resulting in a continuous spectrum of light appearing in the sky.
Named for its type genus, this plant family of nearly 4,800 species includes the trees and shrubs behind apples, pears, plums, cherries, and peaches — what family is it?
Rosaceae is a family of flowering plants that includes 4,828 known species in 91 genera.

Seven living species make up this group of ocean-dwelling reptiles, five of which are threatened with extinction — one species, found only near Australia, Papua New Guinea, and Indonesia, is not — name this group?
Sea turtle (superfamily Chelonioidea), sometimes called marine turtles, are reptiles of the order Testudines and of the suborder Cryptodira.
Commonly but inaccurately nicknamed for a big cat it wasn't closely related to, this extinct genus of saber-toothed predator roamed the Americas until as recently as 8,200 years ago — which genus?
Smilodon is a genus of extinct felids. It is one of the best-known saber-toothed predators and prehistoric mammals.
A Canadian cognitive psychologist at Harvard who champions evolutionary psychology and the computational theory of mind, which popular-science author wrote on how children learn irregular verb forms?
Steven Pinker (born September 18, 1954) is a Canadian cognitive psychologist, psycholinguist, popular science author, and public intellectual.
Born in 1946, this American serial killer often posed as an authority figure or feigned injury to lure young women to his car before assaulting and murdering them — who was he?
Ted Bundy (n Cowell; November 24, 1946 - January 24, 1989) was an American serial killer who kidnapped, raped and murdered dozens of young women and girls throughout 1974, 1975, and 1978.
This metric unit of mass equals exactly 1,000 kilograms — about 2,204.6 pounds — and is technically identical to the SI unit called the megagram. What is it?
Tonne (or; symbol: t) is a unit of mass equal to 1,000 kilograms.
Native to Europe and southwestern Asia, this herbaceous perennial flowering plant is the type species of its genus and a member of the honeysuckle family — which herb?
Valerian (herb) (Valeriana officinalis) is an herbaceous perennial flowering plant in the family Caprifoliaceae, native to Europe and southwestern Asia.
Caused by a mutation in the ATP7B gene, this inherited condition lets copper build up in the liver and brain, leading to tremors, personality changes, and yellowing skin — which condition?
Wilson's disease (also called hepatolenticular degeneration) is a genetic disorder characterized by the excess build-up of copper in the body.
Also known by his Latinized name Rhazes, this Persian polymath authored over 200 manuscripts on medicine, philosophy, and astronomy during the Islamic Golden Age — who was he?
Abu Bakr al-Razi: 10th-century Iranian physician and polymath.
Based on a civilian widebody jet, this European aerial-refueling tanker holds over 90% of the air-to-air refueling market outside the United States, with 17 countries as customers — which aircraft?

Airbus A330 MRTT: Aerial refuelling tanker aircraft. The Airbus A330 Multi Role Tanker Transport (MRTT) is a European aerial refueling and military transport aircraft based on the civilian Airbus A330.
About one-third the density of steel, this soft, nonmagnetic, silver-looking metal grows a protective oxide skin the instant it meets air — which element, symbol Al?
Aluminium: Chemical element with atomic number 13 (Al)
Triggered by either histamine or bradykinin, this rapid swelling of the deep skin layers can affect the face, tongue, or airway within minutes — what is it?
Angioedema: Disease characterized by rapid swelling.

Once mistaken for bacteria, this domain of single-celled organisms is now known to be the group from which eukaryotes evolved, distinguished by ether-linked cell membranes and a unique whip-like motility structure. What domain is it?
Archaea: Domain of organisms. Traditionally, Archaea included only its prokaryotic members, but has since been found to be paraphyletic, as eukaryotes are known to have evolved from archaea.
Affecting roughly one in five people at some point and usually starting in childhood, this long-term itchy, red, cracked-skin condition is also simply called eczema — what's its formal name?
Atopic dermatitis: Long-term form of skin inflammation.
A blood-feeding parasite of the genus Cimex that usually bites at night, this insect leaves itchy welts but, reassuringly, isn't known to spread any infectious disease — what is it?
Bed bug: Type of insect that feeds on human blood.
Despite its name, only the soles of this tawny, spotted feline's paws are actually dark — and at just 35 to 52 centimetres long, it ranks as Africa's smallest wild feline species — what animal is it?
Black-footed cat: Small wild cat native to Southern Africa.
Rooted in prehistoric herbalism for identifying edible and medicinal species, this branch of biology studies roughly 410,000 species of land plants — what field of study?
Named from the Greek word for butter, this oily, foul-smelling compound with the formula CH3CH2CH2COOH is a key component of the mammalian gut. What is it?
Butyric acid: Chemical compound (CH3CH2CH2COOH). It is an oily, colorless liquid with an unpleasant odor.
These biomolecules often follow the tidy empirical formula (CH2O)n, and as polysaccharides like starch, glycogen, and cellulose they store energy and build structure — what family are they?
Carbohydrate: Organic compound that consists only of carbon, hydrogen, and oxygen.
Consisting mainly of the brain and spinal cord — and, surprisingly, the retina too — this part of the body integrates information to coordinate an animal's activity — what is it?
Central nervous system: Brain and spinal cord. The rest of this article exclusively discusses the vertebrate central nervous system, which is radically distinct from all other animals.
Sold as Thorazine, this drug was the first of the typical antipsychotics — used to treat schizophrenia and, oddly, hiccups that won't quit. What is it?
Their 'lady' actually refers to the Virgin Mary, and their cheerful red-and-black warning colours tell predators they taste terrible — what is this 6,000-species family of small beetles?
Coccinellidae: Family of beetles. The more than 6,000 described species have a global distribution and are found in a variety of habitats.
First created near Darmstadt in 1996 and named for an astronomer on his 537th anniversary, this synthetic element (number 112) is so volatile it may even be a gas — which element?
Copernicium: Chemical element with atomic number 112 (Cn)
Caused by prolonged exposure to excess cortisol, this condition produces abdominal weight gain with thin limbs, a rounded red face, and reddish stretch marks — which condition is it?
Cushing's syndrome: Symptoms from excessive exposure to glucocorticoids such as cortisol.

Known mainly through DNA evidence rather than plentiful fossils, this extinct archaic human group ranged across Asia until about 32,000 years ago, and DNA analysis confirmed the Harbin skull belonged to it — what group is it?
Denisovan: Archaic human species from Asia.
In 1949, this NASA mathematician became the first African-American woman to supervise a team at Langley, later teaching herself and her staff the Fortran language — who is she?
Dorothy Vaughan: American human computer and computer programmer (1910–2008)
This group of 13 genetic connective tissue disorders causes loose joints and stretchy, velvety skin, with a classification last updated in 2017 — what condition is it?
Ehlers–Danlos syndrome: Group of genetic connective tissues disorders. The existing classification was last updated in 2017, when a number of rarer forms of EDS were added.
Despite never earning a university degree, this German-American psychoanalyst taught at Harvard, Berkeley, and Yale, and coined the term 'identity crisis' — who is he?
Erik Erikson: American psychoanalyst and essayist (1902–1994)

With a red face, a black-and-white head, and a bold yellow wing bar, this small finch native to the Palearctic often appears in Italian Renaissance paintings of the Madonna and Child. What bird is it?
European goldfinch: Species of bird. It has been introduced to other areas, including Australia, New Zealand, Uruguay and the United States.
Also known as the bodhi tree, this species is revered in four South Asian religions as the tree beneath which Buddha is said to have reached enlightenment — which species?
Ficus religiosa: Species of fig. Ficus religiosa or sacred fig is a species of fig native to the Indian subcontinent and Indochina that belongs to Moraceae, the fig or mulberry family.
Known online by the alias TiAMO, this Swede co-founded a notorious file-sharing site and stood trial for it in 2009, a saga captured in the documentary TPB AFK — who is he?
This mathematician founded set theory and proved that there are more real numbers than natural numbers, revealing an infinity of infinities — who is he?
Known online by the alias 'anakata,' this Swedish computer specialist co-founded a notorious BitTorrent site and later helped WikiLeaks with its 2010 release of a leaked military video — who is he?
Gottfrid Svartholm: Swedish computer specialist. Parts of an interview with Svartholm commenting on the May 2006 police raid of The Pirate Bay are featured in Good Copy Bad Copy and Steal This Film.
Nicknamed the slime eel, this jawless marine scavenger is the only living animal with a skull but no proper backbone — what is it?
Hagfish: Class of eel-shaped, slime-producing animal.

Famous for the ideas of "bounded rationality" and "satisficing," this remarkable scholar won both a Turing Award and a Nobel in Economics — bridging computer science, economics, and psychology. Who was he?
Herbert A. Simon: American academic and Nobel Laureate (1916–2001)

Found only in the Americas from Alaska to Tierra del Fuego, these roughly 375 species pull off rapid, maneuverable flight thanks to an exceptional metabolism — and their males flaunt the widest plumage diversity of any bird — what are they?
Named from an Ancient Greek word for 'intestinal obstruction,' this medical condition disrupts the gut's normal propulsive movement, whether from lost peristalsis or a physical blockage — what is it?
Ileus: Disruption to the propulsive ability of the intestine.
A self-taught rocketeer and practicing occultist, this co-founder of both JPL and Aerojet invented the first castable composite rocket propellant before dying young in 1952. Who was he?
Court astronomer and advisor to Elizabeth I, this mathematician-occultist kept one of England's largest libraries and is credited with coining the term "British Empire" — who was he?
John Dee: English scientist and occultist (1527–1608/09)
Convicted in 1995 of fraud and illegally intercepting communications, this hacker served five years in prison before founding his own computer-security consulting firm — who is he?
This probability principle explains why a casino might lose money on a single spin of roulette but reliably earns a predictable percentage over many thousands of spins. What is it called?
Law of large numbers: Averages of repeated trials converge to the expected value.
Instrumental in the discovery of nuclear fission, this Austrian-Swedish physicist fled Nazi Germany in 1938 after losing her post under the Nuremberg Laws — who is she?

Fired by IBM in 1968 for revealing her intent to transition — an apology that took until 2020 — this computer scientist had already invented dynamic instruction handling behind modern out-of-order execution. Who was she?
Lynn Conway: American computer scientist and electrical engineer (1938–2024)

Originally hoping to become an engineer, this Italian physician became one of the first women to graduate from medical school in Italy and later devised an influential educational philosophy — who is she?
Maria Montessori: Italian physician and educator (1870–1952)
Comprising 18 to 24 species that hybridize freely where their ranges overlap, this genus of the mint family thrives in wet, moist soils worldwide — what is it?
Mentha: Genus of flowering plants in the family Lamiaceae.
NATO nicknames it 'Foxhound,' and at roughly 3,000 km/h it's the fastest operational combat aircraft known — which interceptor, a Soviet successor to the MiG-25, is it?
Mikoyan MiG-31: Interceptor aircraft. The MiG-31 is the fastest known operational combat aircraft, with a top speed around 3,000 km/h (1,600 knots).
Built with a slender segmented body and a long piercing-and-sucking proboscis, this family of 3,600 fly species diversified back in the Cretaceous — what are they?
Mosquito: Family of flies. The word mosquito (formed by mosca and diminutive -ito) is Spanish and Portuguese for little fly.

This branch of alternative medicine rests on vitalism and folk healing rather than evidence, and its grab-bag of 'natural' methods runs from the thoroughly discredited to certain accepted psychotherapies. What is it?
Naturopathy: Form of alternative medicine. The ethics of naturopathy have been called into question by medical professionals and its practice has been characterized as quackery.
Nicknamed the 'winter vomiting disease' and spread by the fecal-oral route, this is the most common cause of gastroenteritis — what is it?
Norovirus: Type of viruses that cause gastroenteritis.

Numbering 126 species, these are the largest order of marsupials in the Western Hemisphere — and only one of them, the Virginia variety, made it as far north as the United States and Canada. What animal is this?
Nicknamed the 'white rats' of its phylum for how often it's cultivated in classrooms and labs, this single-celled ciliate thrives in stagnant ponds — what is it?
This nerve-damage condition can be triggered by diabetes, vitamin B12 deficiency, or certain chemotherapy and antibiotic drugs, and may come on suddenly or creep in slowly — what is it?
Peripheral neuropathy: Nervous system disease affecting nerves beyond the brain and spinal cord.
This French physicist shared the 1903 Nobel Prize in Physics with his wife, making them the first married couple to win a Nobel — who is he?
Pierre Curie: French physicist and chemist (1859–1906)
Also called quaking aspen for the way its leaves flutter in the slightest breeze, which poplar species is native to the Old World's cool temperate regions?
Nicknamed 'gold cap' and 'golden halo,' this is the world's best-known psilocybin-containing mushroom thanks to its wide distribution and how easily it's cultivated — which species?
Psilocybe cubensis: Species of fungus. It belongs to the fungus family Hymenogastraceae and was previously known as Stropharia cubensis.
Also known as steelhead in its sea-run form, this North American Pacific species shows off a vivid reddish stripe along its flank in breeding males — which fish?
Rainbow trout: Fresh-water species of fish.
His 'Essai Sur La Nature Du Commerce' was called the 'cradle of political economy'; this Irish-French banker made a fortune speculating in John Law's Mississippi Company — who is it?
Richard Cantillon: Irish-French economist and banker (c. 1680 – 1734)
This light Swedish single-engine supersonic fighter has a delta wing and canard configuration with fly-by-wire controls and is fully NATO interoperable — what is it?
Saab JAS 39 Gripen: Light single-engined multirole fighter aircraft from Sweden.
Distinguished from true seals by external ear flaps and the ability to walk on all fours, these marine mammals include a giant subspecies that can weigh up to 1,000 kilograms. What are they?
Sea lion: Subfamily of aquatic mammals.

Composed of repeating siloxane units with a backbone of oxygen and silicon rather than carbon, this synthetic material fills sealants, cookware, and medical devices, and is often confused with the chip-making element it's named after — what is it?
Native to the Andes, this is the only living species in South America from the short-faced lineage, and unlike most of its relatives, eats mostly plants — which animal?
Spectacled bear: Species of mammal. The spectacled bear (Tremarctos ornatus), also known as the Andean bear, is a species of bear native to the Andes Mountains in northern and western South America.

Named after a Scottish village where it was discovered in 1790, this alkaline earth metal was first isolated in 1808 by Humphry Davy using electrolysis, and identified a year after its discovery by its crimson-red flame test. What element is it?
Strontium: Chemical element with atomic number 38 (Sr)
Known by folk names like bitter buttons and golden buttons, this Eurasian flowering plant in the daisy family has become invasive after being introduced to Australia and the Americas — which plant?
Tansy: Species of plant. Tansy (Tanacetum vulgare) is a perennial, herbaceous flowering plant in the genus Tanacetum in the family Asteraceae, native to temperate Europe and Asia.
This body region between the hip and the knee contains a single bone — the femur — that forms a ball-and-socket joint above and a hinge joint below. What is it?
Thigh: Body part between pelvis and knee; upper leg.
Caused by the parasite Toxoplasma gondii and often spread through undercooked meat or infected cat feces, this disease is famously dangerous to catch during pregnancy — what is it?
Normally containing two arteries and one vein cushioned in Wharton's jelly, this conduit links a developing fetus to the placenta — what is it?
Umbilical cord: Conduit between embryo/fetus and the placenta.

Most animals make their own, but humans, guinea pigs, and some bats must eat it because a synthesis-enzyme gene is broken; this citrus nutrient builds collagen and acts as an antioxidant — what is it?
Vitamin C: Essential nutrient found in citrus fruits and other foods.
Ranging from a few meters for Bluetooth to millions of kilometers for deep-space signals, this method of sending information relies on radio waves instead of cables -- what is it called?
Wireless: Transfer of information or power that does not require the use of physical wires.
Tellurium is denoted by which symbol?
The symbol for tellurium is Te. Tellurium is a chemical element; it has the symbol Te and atomic number 52.
Darmstadtium is denoted by which symbol?
The symbol for darmstadtium is Ds. Darmstadtium is a synthetic chemical element; it has symbol Ds and atomic number 110.

F. Murray Abraham (born 1939) is the earliest of the four. Murray Abraham (born Murray Abraham; October 24, 1939) is an American actor.

Paul Lynde (born 1926) is the earliest of the four.

Michael Trucco (born 1970) is the earliest of the four.

The Third Man (founded 1948) is the earliest of the four.

Stranger Things (released 2016) is the earliest of the four.

Mighty Morphin Power Rangers: Once & Always
Ocean Waves (released 1993) is the earliest of the four.

Heavy Metal (film) (released 1981) is the earliest of the four.
Which of these four is a comedian?
Richard Ayoade is a comedian. Richard Ayoade ( EYE-oh-AH-dee; born 23 May 1977) is a British comedian, actor, writer, director, and presenter.
In what year was Lily James born?
Lily James: Lily Chloe Ninette Thomson (born 5 April 1989), known professionally as Lily James, is an English actress.
In what year was Serge Gainsbourg born?
Serge Gainsbourg (French: [sɛʁʒ(ə) ɡɛ̃zbuʁ]; born Lucien Ginsburg; 2 April 1928 – 2 March 1991) was a French singer-songwriter, actor, composer, and director.
In what year was Amanda Seyfried born?
Amanda Seyfried: Amanda Michelle Seyfried ( SY-fred; born December 3, 1985) is an American actress.
